title: Build a Semantic Layout
question: Rewrite index.html so the page uses semantic landmarks: a <header> with a <nav>, a single <main>, and a <footer>. Keep the same text content.

files.index.html:
My Site

Home About

Welcome to my site.

© 2024
files.styles.css:
body { font-family: system-ui; padding: 16px; }
nav a, .links a { margin-right: 8px; }

solutionCode:
My Site

Home About

Welcome to my site.

© 2024
exampleOutput: Same page rendered with header/nav/main/footer landmarks.
hints: A page should contain exactly one <main> landmark.
bruteForce: Leaving everything as <div> is valid HTML but conveys no structure to assistive tech or search engines.
optimal: Semantic landmarks populate the accessibility tree with roles for free — no ARIA needed.

title: Give Images Alt Text
question: Each in index.html is missing its alt attribute. Add a descriptive alt to the content image and an empty alt="" to the decorative divider so screen readers handle each correctly.

files.styles.css:
body { font-family: system-ui; padding: 16px; }
img { display: block; }

constraints: Every must have an alt attribute (decorative images use alt="").
hints: Content images need descriptive alt text.
Purely decorative images should have alt="" so screen readers skip them.
bruteForce: Omitting alt makes screen readers announce the file name or nothing useful.
optimal: Descriptive alt for content, empty alt for decoration — the two correct patterns.

title: Make an Accessible Table
question: Turn the bare table into an accessible data table: add a <caption>, wrap the header row in <thead>, and give each header cell scope="col".
exampleOutput: A captioned table with a proper header row and scoped headers.
hints: The header row's cells should be <th scope="col">, not <td>.
<caption> names the table; <thead>/<tbody> group the rows.
bruteForce: A table of only <td> cells gives screen readers no way to associate data with headers.
optimal: Caption + thead + scoped th cells make the relationships explicit to assistive tech.

title: Label Every Form Control
question: The form's inputs have no labels (only placeholders). Associate a <label> with each input using for/id, so the controls are accessible.

files.index.html:
<form>
  <input type="text" placeholder="Your name">
  <input type="email" placeholder="Email">
  <button type="submit">Sign up</button>
</form>

solutionCode:
<form>
  <label for="name">Your name</label>
  <input id="name" type="text">
  <label for="email">Email</label>
  <input id="email" type="email">
  <button type="submit">Sign up</button>
</form>
exampleOutput: Each input has a visible, associated label.
constraints: Every control must have a <label> (via for/id or wrapping).
hints: Give each input an id, then point a <label for="thatId"> at it.
A placeholder is not a label — it disappears on input and isn't reliably announced.
bruteForce: Relying on placeholder text alone leaves controls without accessible names.
optimal: Explicit <label for> associations give every control a stable accessible name.

title: Fix the Heading Outline
question: This page has a broken heading order (it skips levels and uses the wrong level for the title). Rewrite it to a logical outline: exactly one <h1>, then <h2>, then <h3>, with no skipped levels.
exampleOutput: A single h1 followed by h2 and h3 with no skipped levels.
constraints: Exactly one <h1>; do not skip heading levels.
hints: The page title should be the single <h1>.
Pick heading levels by document structure, not font size — style with CSS.
bruteForce: Choosing headings for their default size produces an outline that confuses screen readers and crawlers.
optimal: One h1 and a level-by-level hierarchy conveys the document's true structure.
